chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
title: Theaters on the circuit: RKO houses and Philadelphia's Black theaters
summary: He recalls theaters in Cleveland, Boston and Philadelphia, including Sam Steeple's Lincoln, Pearl and Nixon Grand.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Name some of the theaters you played, Butter.
We played all the RKO theaters and we used to double back. Like when we played the RKO Palace in Cleveland, we would come back maybe three months later and play Loew's Orpheum in the same town.
Uh-huh. Well, a lot of times you played RKO theaters in ? What other towns
Oh, gee whiz, Cleveland. We played Youngstown, --
We played at the Metropolitan in Boston.
And where'd you play in Philadelphia? The Earl? Was it the Earl?
No, we didn't play the Earl Theater. No, we didn't play that. We played I think it was the Lincoln Theater then, which was a colored house in those days.
Sam Steeple owned the Lincoln. In fact he owned a chain of theaters in Philadelphia. He owned the Pearl Theater, he owned the Nixon Grand.
The Pearl Theater in Philadelphia is where a lot of great black stars got a start?

Exactly, out on Ridge Avenue it was. That's the first theater I ever played, by the way, with McKinney's Cottonpickers in my life. The first day I ever played in my life was the Pearl Theater in Philadelphia.
Name some of the great people that got started there. Dizzy -- I think Dizzy played there first.

I don't think Dizzy played there because I think the Pearl was closed when Dizzy came. When Dizzy came to Philadelphia he was -- when he was with Frankie Fairfax, I think the Pearl had closed then. But the Nixon Grand was open, the Lincoln was open, and they used to have all the -- have the black shows, you see, and the black bands. All the big bands used to play there.
